strengths: The core idea of employing reinforcement learning (specifically GRPO) to jointly optimize task performance and token sparsity/efficiency during post-training is sensible and timely for MLLMs.
The proposed formulation is lightweight and plug-and-play, avoiding architectural redesign or pre-training from scratch by building on dynamic sparse attention (ZipVL).
Empirical evaluation covers a broad set of 13 benchmarks across both image and video modalities on multiple modern base models (Qwen2-VL and Qwen2.5-VL series).
weaknesses: The manuscript is severely underdeveloped in length and depth (under 4 pages of content excluding references), reading more like an extended abstract or workshop proposal than a complete conference paper.

No actual wall-clock speedup or memory footprint measurements (such as time-to-first-token, prefill latency, decoding throughput, or peak GPU memory) are provided. Reporting only the theoretical 'token ratio' is insufficient to validate real-world deployment acceleration.

There is an internal contradiction regarding the sampling of parameter p: Section 2.2 states each response is generated with a random threshold drawn uniformly from U(0, 1), whereas Section 3 states that p is restricted to the range [0.94, 0.975] with a step size of 0.005.

Lack of essential ablation studies: the paper does not analyze the impact of the efficiency reward formulation, the relative weighting between performance and efficiency rewards, the effect of the KL divergence penalty, or the training convergence behavior and computational cost.

Missing in-depth analysis of why and how the method works. For the exact same retention threshold (p = 0.975), ZipVL keeps ~75-80% of tokens while ZipR1 keeps only ~22-25% tokens. The paper provides no attention entropy visualizations, attention distribution analysis, or qualitative examples to explain this dramatic shift in attention behavior.

strengths: The core idea of using reinforcement learning (specifically GRPO) to encourage sharper attention and higher token sparsity during post-training is conceptually intuitive and interesting.
The paper evaluates across a wide variety of standard multimodal benchmarks (7 image and 6 video benchmarks) with multiple model scales (Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-3B, and Qwen2.5-VL-7B).
weaknesses: Extremely incomplete submission: The paper spans only 4 pages of main content, lacking the standard depth, analysis, and discussion expected for a top-tier AI conference paper.

Lack of actual latency, throughput, and memory measurements: Although efficiency is the central claim and motivation of the paper, only the proxy metric 'token ratio' is reported. There are no wall-clock speedups, decoding latency benchmarks, prefilling time measurements, or real GPU peak memory measurements presented.

Inconsistencies and lack of technical clarity: In Section 2.2, the text states that thresholds are sampled as $p_n \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1)$, whereas Section 3 states that $p$ is sampled within $[0.94, 0.975]$ with a step size of $0.005$. Furthermore, the paper does not clearly explain the physical mechanism behind how the token ratio decreases from ~75% to ~23% under the exact same inference threshold ($p = 0.975$)—presumably through learned attention sharpening, but no attention entropy/distribution visualizations or analysis are provided to substantiate this.

Complete lack of ablation studies and baselines: The paper only compares against the base model and ZipVL. There are no comparisons against other vision-language token pruning/sparsification methods (e.g., FastV, Vision-Zip, SparseVLM), nor are there ablations on reward weighting (e.g., varying the balance between $r_{\text{per}}$ and $r_{\text{eff}}$), group size $N$, reference model KL penalty $\beta$, or threshold sampling distributions.

Insufficient training and implementation details: Essential training hyperparameters (e.g., optimizer, learning rate, schedule, batch size, number of training steps/epochs, hardware infrastructure, and training time) are omitted, severely hindering reproducibility.

strengths: The core idea of using reinforcement learning (GRPO) with a joint performance and efficiency reward to post-train MLLMs for enhanced attention sparsity is intuitive and elegant.
Comprehensive evaluation across 13 diverse benchmarks covering both image and video modalities (e.g., MME, MMBench, TextVQA, VideoMME, PerceptionTest).

Evaluated on strong and modern open-source vision-language backbones, including Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-3B, and Qwen2.5-VL-7B, demonstrating consistent token ratio reduction from ~75-80% down to ~22-24% with minimal accuracy degradation.
weaknesses: The submission is extremely brief (only 4 pages of text) and resembles an extended abstract or workshop preprint rather than a complete, competitive conference submission.

No actual wall-clock speedup, inference latency, or peak GPU memory measurements are reported. Token ratio is an informative proxy, but sparse attention kernels often suffer from non-trivial overheads; empirical throughput and latency numbers across prefilling and decoding are necessary to substantiate deployment claims.

Critical ablation studies are missing. The paper lacks analyses on the balance between performance and efficiency rewards (e.g., varying weights between $r_{\text{per}}$ and $r_{\text{eff}}$), the effect of the KL penalty $\beta$, the impact of group size $N$ in GRPO, and comparison against standard supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with sparsity regularization.

There is an inconsistency in the description of the sparsity threshold $p$: Section 2.2 states $p_n \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1)$ is sampled to generate diverse responses, whereas Section 3 states '$p$ is set within the range of [0.94, 0.975] with a step size of 0.005'.

Missing qualitative and analytical insights: The paper does not visualize how attention maps or token retention distributions evolve across layers and modalities after RL training, leaving the underlying mechanism unexplored.

strengths: Innovative formulation that applies grouped reinforcement learning (GRPO) directly to the accuracy-efficiency trade-off, treating token reduction ratio and answer correctness as joint rewards rather than relying on proxy attention-sharpening objectives.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning thirteen image and video benchmarks across four model checkpoints (Qwen2-VL-7B, Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B, LLaVA-Video-7B), consistently outperforming prior training-free and trainable sparse attention baselines at aggressive compression ratios.
Significant practical benefits demonstrated with actual inference latency speedups (up to 3.3x) and memory savings (up to 3.0x), rather than relying solely on theoretical FLOPs calculations.

Insightful analysis showing that post-training naturally sharpens the attention distribution, allowing the model to hit top-p retention thresholds with substantially fewer tokens while maintaining robustness on hallucination diagnostics (HallusionBench).
weaknesses: Notational and procedural inconsistency regarding the threshold sampling during training: Section 3.2 describes sampling $p_n \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1)$, whereas Section 4 specifies $p \in [0.94, 0.975]$ with a step size of 0.005. The paper should clearly harmonize these descriptions.

Training efficiency and scalability constraints: Because each candidate threshold $p$ induces a distinct attention mask and KV-cache trajectory, rollout generation cannot be easily batched across different $p$ values within a group, leading to sequential execution overhead that could hinder scaling to larger foundation models.

Limited evaluation on long-form generative tasks: The benchmarks tested are predominantly multiple-choice or short-form visual QA where $|o| \ll |x|$; it remains less clear how aggressively pruned KV caches affect long-context multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning.

strengths: Well-motivated and novel post-training framework: Formulating token sparsity optimization as a reinforcement learning problem using GRPO is an elegant and effective alternative to rigid heuristic pruning or proxy attention-sharpening regularizers.

Well-crafted reward mechanism: The inclusion of the group-level correctness indicator $C$ in the joint reward function effectively prevents policy collapse toward degenerate ultra-sparse solutions when all rollouts in a group fail.

Thorough empirical evaluation: The method is validated across 13 diverse vision and video benchmarks and across multiple backbones (Qwen2-VL, Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA-Video), demonstrating substantial token reduction (down to ~24-29% retained tokens) with negligible performance drop.

Comprehensive supporting analyses: The paper provides informative ablations on attention mechanisms (top-$k$ vs. top-$p$), budget sweep ranges, hallucination impact via HallusionBench, and real inference wall-clock latency/memory improvements.
weaknesses: Training computational overhead: The rollout generation under different budget thresholds $p$ induces distinct retention masks and KV-cache trajectories, preventing batching and requiring sequential execution. The manuscript acknowledges this limitation but does not report the total training wall-clock time or GPU hours compared to standard SFT/RL baselines.

Limited evaluation of post-training baselines: The comparison with trainable sparse attention baselines (MOBA, Sharpness loss) in Table 3 is conducted on only one model (Qwen2.5-VL-7B) across 4 benchmarks, whereas the main comparison in Tables 1-2 only covers training-free methods.

Applicability beyond benchmark QA: The performance reward relies on verifiable binary correctness ($r_{\text{per}} \in \{0, 1\}$). How this RL framework generalizes to open-ended multimodal generation or complex instruction following without ground-truth answers remains underexplored.

Clarity on inference behavior: The explanation of how fixing $p=0.975$ at test time yields ~24% token retention after training (compared to ~75% before training) could be made clearer in the main text by explicitly highlighting the shift in attention distribution sharpness.

strengths: Novel and intuitive formulation: Casting token sparsity as an explicit reinforcement learning objective using GRPO directly addresses the performance-efficiency trade-off, bridging the mismatch between training and inference seen in prior SFT- or regularizer-based approaches.
Well-designed reward mechanism: The inclusion of a group correctness indicator (Equation 8) to gate efficiency rewards prevents policy collapse into trivial ultra-sparse but incorrect answers.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: The method is tested across 13 standard image and video benchmarks (e.g., VideoMME, MMStar, ChartQA, MMMU-Pro) and multiple model architectures (Qwen2-VL, Qwen2.5-VL, LLaVA-Video-7B), consistently demonstrating significant token reduction (down to ~23-26%) with minimal performance drop compared to standard attention.

Meaningful inference acceleration and resource savings: The paper validates real-world system benefits, showing up to 3.3x prefill/decoding speedups and 3x KV-cache memory reductions at long sequence lengths.

Thorough ablations: The authors provide helpful ablations on sparsity mechanisms (top-k vs. threshold vs. top-p), hyperparameter exploration ($p$ range and group size), layer-wise sparsity behavior, and hallucination robustness on HallusionBench.
weaknesses: Inconsistency in description of threshold sampling: In Section 3.2, the method is introduced as sampling $p_n \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1)$, whereas Section 4 specifies a much narrower range of $p \in [0.94, 0.975]$ with discrete step sizes. Clarifying this in the methodology section would avoid confusion.

Lack of detail on answer correctness verification: The paper specifies a binary accuracy reward $r_{\text{per}} \in \{0, 1\}$, but does not detail how correctness is verified across the training sets (e.g., exact match, rule-based parsing, or model-based evaluation), which is critical for reproducibility.

Training efficiency and cost: As noted in the limitations, each budget level produces distinct KV cache and mask patterns, preventing straightforward batching during rollouts and necessitating sequential execution. Providing concrete training wall-clock times and GPU-hour overhead would offer a clearer picture of practical post-training feasibility.

Limited post-training baseline comparisons: While Table 1 and 2 thoroughly compare against training-free sparsification across 13 benchmarks, comparisons against post-training baselines (MOBA and sharpness regularization in Table 3) are restricted to four benchmarks on a single model.
